Learning Objectives
Describe the risk factors for brachial plexus birth injury.
Review the anatomy of the brachial plexus.
Understand the diagnostic tests and physical examination for an infant in whom brachial
plexus birth injury is suspected.
Understand the indications for primary and secondary surgery in patients with brachial plexus
birth injury.

Brachial plexus birth injury (BPBI) refers to an injury sustained to the brachial plexus during
birth.

Overview
BPBI frequently has been described as brachial plexus birth palsy, neonatal brachial
plexus palsy, obstetrical brachial plexus injury or palsy, perinatal brachial plexus injury,
among other terms. The hypothesized mechanism of injury is a widening angle between
the neck and shoulder of a newborn as it passes through the birth canal.1 Factors that
increase the risk for BPBI are shoulder dystocia, large newborns with a birthweight
greater than 3,500 g, fetopelvic disproportion, instrumented birth, single and multiple
natural births, and gestational diabetes mellitus.1-4 Cesarean delivery is negatively
correlated with BPBI; however, it does not eliminate the possibility of injury.2 Large
database studies have shown a decrease in BPBI from 1.7 in 1,000 births in 1997 to 0.9 in
1,000 births 2012.2,3 BPBI resolves spontaneously in approximately 75% of patients.5
Management may vary and depends on time of treatment referral, injury pattern, and
clinical presentation.
Epidemiology
The incidence has been reported to be 1 to 4 per 1,000 live births.1-4

Epidemiology
Early retrospective case reports established the incidence as approximately 2 in 1,000
births between 1972 and 1982.6 Subsequent studies by Foad et al3 and Defrancesco et
al2 established an incidence of 1.7 in 1,000 live births to 0.9 in 1,000 live births in the
United States between 1997 and 2012. A state database study that examined
consecutive data over 15 years reported a similar proportional decrease in incidence
from 0.82 in 1,000 births to 0.56 in 1,000 births.4 The right side is more frequently
affected than the left side.6 Changes in birthing techniques, awareness of maternal
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:34 AM
AAOS | Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001054
2/21

health, and awareness of BPBI and shoulder dystocia appear to have decreased the risk
of injury.1,2,4
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The brachial plexus consists of nerve root contributions from C5 to T1 (Figure 1).
Pre-fixed cord with contribution from C4 in 22%
Post-fixed cord with contribution from T1 in 1%
C5 and C6 nerve roots form the upper trunk
The Erb point is the site at the upper trunk of the brachial plexus at which the suprascapular
nerve begins. It is the most common location of a brachial plexus birth injury.
C7 nerve root forms the middle trunk
C8 and T1 nerve roots form the lower trunk
Each trunk then divides into an anterior and posterior division.
The divisions then combine to form the medial, lateral, and posterior cords.
The cords then divide to become individual peripheral nerves.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:34 AM
AAOS | Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001054
3/21

Figure 1 Illustration of the brachial plexus. (Adapted from Thompson WO, Warren RF, Barnes RP,
Hunt S: Shoulder injuries, in Schenck RC Jr, ed: Athletic Training and Sports Medicine, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 1999, pp 219-291.)
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The etiology of BPBI is thought to be the result of birth trauma caused by mechanical traction
to the nerves of the brachial plexus.7,8

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Shoulder dystocia is the greatest cause of BPBI.2-4 As a newborn passes through the
birth canal, traction may be applied across the shoulder and neck during delivery of the
newborn’s head, which results in an injury to the brachial plexus. Fetopelvic
disproportion, delivery position, and large newborns are associated with an increased
risk of brachial plexus injury. Some studies have suggested that fetal distress may cause
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:34 AM
AAOS | Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001054
4/21

hypotonia, leading to an increased risk of nerve stretch injuries during the birthing
process.
Risk Factors
Risk factors include macrosomia, Fetopelvic disproportion, maternal gestational diabetes
mellitus, shoulder dystocia/difficult delivery, prior deliveries associated with BPBI, prolonged
labor, multiparous pregnancies, and breech delivery2-4 (Resource 1).

Risk Factors
The greatest risk factor for BPBI is shoulder dystocia, in which one or both shoulders are
stuck inside the mother’s pelvis during labor while the head is being delivered through
the birth canal. National database studies report that newborns with macrosomia or a
birthweight of 4,500 g or more are the second greatest risk factors for BPBI;2,3 however,
these studies consider birthweight a binary variable, which categorizes very large and
heavy newborns at greatest risk for BPBI. A smaller database study that included more
than 900,000 birthweights reported that BPBI risk increased in frequency at
approximately 3,500 g, with a mean birthweight of 3,800 g. Every 50-g increase in
birthweight led to a 7% increased risk of BPBI.4 Instrumented birth with the use of
forceps is the third most common cause of BPBI, with an odds ratio of 9 to 21, whereas
the odds ratio of vacuum-assisted birth as a cause of BPBI ranged from 2.7 to 7.7.2-4
Breech delivery, gestational diabetes mellitus, birth hypoxia, and natural birth tend to be
associated with odds ratios of 5 or less but may substantially contribute to BPBI risk if
present concurrently. The most notable protective factor for BPBI is caesarean delivery.2-
4
Associated Injuries
Clavicle or humerus fractures
Glenohumeral dysplasia
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:34 AM
AAOS | Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001054
5/21


Associated Injuries
Clavicle fractures may be difficult to differentiate from BPBI. The incidence of newborn
clavicle fractures is 2 to 3 per 1,000 live births.9,10 Among patients with a BPBI, clavicle
fractures are present in 7.84% of newborns. Gandhi et al9 reported that the presence of
a clavicle fracture and shoulder dystocia did not considerably affect the risk of BPBI
compared with the presence of shoulder dystocia alone (odds ratio, 126.7 versus 112.1,
respectively). In a subgroup analysis, Wall et al10 reported that newborns with a BPBI
and a clavicle fracture were 5% more likely to experience resolution of injury without a
persistent neurologic deficit.
In patients with impaired growth of denervated muscle across the developing shoulder,
progressive dysplasia of the glenohumeral joint occurs, with posterior subluxation of the
humeral head, humeral head flattening, and increased glenoid retroversion.
Injury Classification
BPBI may be classified according to the anatomic levels of involvement (eg, upper trunk, lower
trunk, total plexus)5 (Resource 2).
The upper trunk (C5-C6) of the brachial plexus is the most commonly injured; this also is
classically known as Erb's palsy.
An extended upper trunk injury also will involve C7.
Global injuries involve C5 through T1.
An isolated lower trunk injury (C8-T1) is known as Klumpke palsy and is extremely rare in
isolation.
Narakas classification11
Type I: C5 and C6 involvement
Type II: C5, C6 and C7 involvement
Type III: Pan-plexus injury
Type IV: Pan-plexus injury with associated Horner syndrome
Neurologically, injuries may consist of nerve root avulsion, neurotmesis, axonotmesis, and
neurapraxia.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:34 AM
AAOS | Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001054
6/21

Glenohumeral dysplasia is classified according to the Waters classification12
Type I: normal glenoid (<5° difference in retroversion compared with the normal
contralateral side)
Type II: increased glenoid retroversion (>5°; no posterior subluxation of the humeral head)
Type III: increased glenoid retroversion and posterior humeral head subluxation (posterior
subluxation <35%)
Type IV: severe deformity with formation of a pseudoglenoid
Type V: severe flattening of the humeral head and the glenoid; progressive or complete
posterior dislocation of the humeral head
Type VI: complete dislocation of the glenohumeral joint 
Type VII: growth arrest of the proximal aspect of the humerus

Narakas Classification
The Narakas classification is commonly used for BPBI.5 Patients with a type I or type II
injury recover from nerve injuries at higher rates than patients with a type III or type IV
injury. Specifically, Narakas patients with a type I or type II injury experienced biceps
recovery at a rate 19 times higher and complete recovery at a rate 11 times higher than
patients with a type III or type IV injury at a follow-up of 3 months. The Narakas
classification system may be prognostic of recovery; however, persistent nerve deficits
tend to be more common in patients with a Narakas type III or type IV injury.13
Patients with neurapraxia experience full recovery in the first months of life.
Axonotmesis recovery depends on the degree of nerve injury and is more prolonged.
Some children with axonotmesis may experience improved outcomes with surgical
treatment. Patients with neurotmesis will not recover without nerve reconstruction.
Patients with a preganglionic avulsion injury cannot recover because the nerve roots
have completely disconnected from the spinal cord.14
The natural history of brachial plexus birth palsy with incomplete neurologic recovery is
progressive glenohumeral joint deformity because of muscle imbalance. Contracture of
the shoulder internal rotators and adductors versus the weakened external rotators and
abductors results in progressive internal rotation and adduction of the humeral head,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:34 AM
AAOS | Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001054
7/21

which places increased stress along the posterior aspect of the glenoid. These deforming
forces cause increased retroversion of the glenoid and flattening and posterior
subluxation of the humeral head. As the glenoid becomes increasingly retroverted, its
posterior aspect forms a false articulation (pseudoglenoid) with the humeral head.14
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Often diagnosed at the time of delivery
Typically associated with infants who are large for gestational age and prolonged labor, often
requiring delivery assistance with the use of vacuum or forceps
Shoulder dystocia is common.
A flaccid or limp arm is noted.
The limb may rest in an adducted, internally rotated position.
Associated Horner syndrome may be present, indicating a preganglionic injury.
Physical Examination
Serial examinations are important to assess neurologic recovery.
Passive range of motion
Particular attention is paid to assessing passive external rotation of the shoulder with the
arm in adduction to evaluate for glenohumeral dysplasia
Active range of motion and strength evaluation
The Active Movement Scale15 is the most used and validated physical examination tool for
tracking neurologic recovery16 (Table 1).
Strength is graded on a 0 to 7 scale, with grades 0 to 4 as active movement with gravity
eliminated and grades 5 to 7 as active movement against gravity. Each increase in level
requires demonstration of motion at the previous level.17
Assess for signs of pre-ganglionic injury (Resource 3).
Horner syndrome
Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, enophthalmos
Phrenic nerve palsy
Elevated hemidiaphragm

Flail hand
Loss of scapular control
Joint contractures are noted and managed via occupational or physical therapy.
The Mallet score may be used for older individuals if they are able to follow commands.18,19

Imaging Studies
Radiography

10/21

May be performed to assess for fractures at birth (humerus or clavicle fractures)20
Pseudoparalysis may result from concomitant fracture.20
If loss of motion persists after the fracture heals, then a diagnosis of BPBI can be made.
Computed Tomography
Typically, CT is not indicated in the diagnosis of BPBI.21
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may be performed in infancy to help determine the severity of the injury and to aid in
surgical planning (nerve transfers versus nerve reconstruction).22
MRI also typically is performed in children older than 1 year to assess for the presence and
severity of glenohumeral dysplasia.12,23
Ultrasonography
Performed in the first 12 months of life (before humeral head ossification) to diagnose
glenohumeral subluxation or dislocation24
The alpha angle5 (Figure 3) and the percentage of humeral head anterior to the mid-scapular
line5 (Figure 4) are important indicators of glenohumeral dysplasia and may aid in
management.

Not often used because they are not well tolerated in young children
Unreliable and often underestimate the severity of injury25
Differential Diagnosis

Pseudoparalysis from associated fracture (humerus or clavicle fracture)
Congenital radial nerve palsy
Spinal cord pathology
Congenital differences
Neuromuscular conditions
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Passive range of motion for all joints in the affected extremity should begin as soon as
possible.5
Loss of shoulder external rotation is an indicator that the child is at risk for internal rotation
contracture and subsequent shoulder subluxation or dislocation.12
Surgical Management
Indications
Indications for microsurgery remain controversial.26 Currently, most studies recommend
exploration and brachial plexus reconstruction for27:
Lack of return of antigravity elbow flexion by 6 months of age28
Flail extremity (total plexus injury) in patients aged 3 months with Horner syndrome

Indications
Return of antigravity elbow flexion strength is a key factor in determining the need for
brachial plexus exploration and nerve reconstruction. A longer delay in the return of
biceps function predicts poorer shoulder outcomes at 5 years and an increased need for
secondary procedures; however, controversy exists with regard to the exact timing of
microsurgical management, with most surgeons recommending this procedure if
antigravity elbow flexion has not returned by age 3 to 9 months.14
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:34 AM
AAOS | Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001054
14/21

Contraindications
Recovery of motor function
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Ultrasonography of the shoulder may be performed if concern for glenohumeral dysplasia
exists so that nerve surgery can be combined with management of the shoulder, such as
closed reduction of the shoulder or Botox of the shoulder internal rotators.5
MRI may be performed to assess for nerve root avulsion injury (pseudomeningocele) to aid
with preoperative planning.25,29
Patient Positioning
The patient typically is placed in the supine position with a bump under the affected shoulder
blade and the head turned to the opposite side to expose the neck.
Both lower extremities typically are prepared and draped if sural nerve grafting is anticipated.
Surgical Approaches30
For avulsion injuries, nerve transfers should be considered.
For nerve ruptures, treatment options include excision of the neuroma and nerve grafting
versus nerve transfers.
Surgical management is performed under general anesthesia without neuromuscular
blockade.
Exposure of the brachial plexus typically is via a transverse skin incision just above the
clavicle.
The platysma and supraclavicular fascia are divided.
The supraclavicular cutaneous nerves and spinal accessory nerve are identified and
protected.
The omohyoid is identified, tagged, and divided.
The transverse cervical vessels are identified and ligated.
The phrenic nerve can be isolated and used as a landmark and traced proximally to identify
C4 and C5 nerve roots.

15/21

Electrical stimulation can verify the identity of the nerve if diaphragmatic contraction is
noted.
C5 and C6 nerve roots exit between the anterior and middle scalene muscles.
Lower roots are sequentially identified.
The subclavian artery is found between the C7 and C8 nerve roots and should be identified
and protected during exploration of the lower plexus.
A second incision below the clavicle generally is necessary for exploration of global plexus
injuries.
The neuroma is identified and isolated.
Somatosensory-evoked potentials can be used intraoperatively to identify nerve root
avulsions.
Surgical strategy of grafting and/or transfers is determined based on exploration of the
neuroma and the results of somatosensory-evoked potential testing.
Secondary procedures
Botulinum toxin injections
Open or arthroscopic reduction of the shoulder joint to decrease glenohumeral dysplasia
(Resource 4)
Tendon transfers: latissimus dorsi and teres major tendon transfers to the rotator cuff; often
combined with releases of the pectoralis major, subscapularis, and coracobrachialis muscles
to improve shoulder abduction and external rotation
Humeral osteotomy with external rotation of the distal humeral segment is recommended in
patients with advanced glenohumeral joint dysplasia.
Glenoid osteotomy can be performed for acute correction of the glenoid deformity; however,
indications for this procedure are still unclear (Video 1).

Outcomes
Prognosis is dependent on the severity of the injury.5
Of all patients, 60% to 90% demonstrate spontaneous recovery.13,31
If antigravity biceps function recovers by 2 months, full recovery is anticipated.
If biceps function recovers at or after 5 months, incomplete recovery is likely.
The presence of Horner syndrome portends a poorer prognosis.
